newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Azeri parliament chief condemns Armenian PM choice.
newsitem.headline: Azeri parliament chief condemns Armenian PM choice.

text.p: A senior Azeri politician condemned on Saturday the naming of the leader of the country's separatist region of Nagorno-Karabakh as the new prime minister of Armenia, Baku's neighbour and foe.

"Armenia has chosen the wrong path. This is a bad sign. They want to legalise the regime in Karabakh, but this will not work. Armenia will achieve nothing," speaker of parliament Murtuz Aleskerov told reporters.
Armenian President Levon Ter-Petrosyan on Thursday announced the surprise appointment of Robert Kocharyan, president of the breakaway Azeri region of Nagorno-Karabakh, as his prime minister.
Diplomats said the move would harm regional peace efforts.

Surrounded by Azeri territory, Karabakh is populated mostly by ethnic Armenians. It broke away from Baku's rule in the late 1980s, triggering years of fighting between Moslem Azeris and Christian Armenians in which thousands were killed. It says it wants independence or union with Armenia proper.
Open war between Azeris and Armenians in and around Karabakh killed thousands before a ceasefire was declared in 1994 after big territorial gains by Karabakh units.
But no political solution to the conflict has been found despite international mediation. Observers say the possibilities for a settlement are worsening.

Aleskerov spoke to reporters at Baku airport before boarding a government plane to Islamabad, where he will represent Azerbaijan in Sunday's meeting of leaders from countries of the Organisation of Islamic Conference (OIC).
He was going as a replacement for President Haydar Aliyev who called off his trip less than a day before he was to depart.
The presidential press service gave no reason for the abrupt cancellation but political observers speculated it was related to Kocharyan's appointment, which clearly caught Azeri leaders off guard.
Aleskerov's comments were the first official reaction.
Nonetheless, when asked if Kocharyan's appointment could threaten the truce, Aleskerov replied: "It cannot".
Political observers in both Azerbaijan and Armenia said the move seemed to indicate that Yerevan had decided to take a harder line on the Karabakh issue.

"I think that this was a surprise for the Azeri government and that it might influence peace negotiations very negatively. It will be much harder to make progress," said one diplomat in Baku on Friday.
He said he thought Ter-Petrosyan, who gave no explanation for his decision to appoint Kocharyan, had acted to pacify nationalist and opposition groups at home.

The 51-year-old leader sent tanks into the streets of the capital Yerevan last year to put down protests by his opponents who accused him of rigging presidential elections. Foreign monitors said the vote was marred by fraud and irregularities.
"Ter-Petrosyan's domestic position has been considerably weakened. He is under great pressure to find common ground with the opposition," said the diplomat.

On Friday Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Armenian officials in Yerevan as saying the appointment of Kocharyan would not have a negative effect on peace talks, provided Azerbaijan did not try to exploit the move for its own benefit.
